identifiers.title: Effect of Sleep Extension on Objectively Assessed Energy Intake Among Adults With Overweight in Real-life Settings: A Randomized Clinical Trial
identifiers.authors: Tasali E, Wroblewski K, Kahn E, Kilkus J, Schoeller DA
identifiers.citation: Tasali E, Wroblewski K, Kahn E, Kilkus J, Schoeller DA. Effect of Sleep Extension on Objectively Assessed Energy Intake Among Adults With Overweight in Real-life Settings: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Intern Med. 2022;182(4):365-374.

design.quote: This single-center, parallel-group RCT was conducted from November 1, 2014, to October 30, 2020.

species.quote: Adult men and women aged 21 to 40 years with a body mass index (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) between 25.0 and 29.9 and a mean habitual sleep duration of less than 6.5 hours per night were eligible.

population.value: Adult men and women aged 21 to 40 years with BMI 25.0 to 29.9 and habitual sleep duration less than 6.5 hours per night
population.quote: Adult men and women aged 21 to 40 years with a body mass index (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) between 25.0 and 29.9 and a mean habitual sleep duration of less than 6.5 hours per night were eligible.

sampleSize.quote: Data from 80 randomized participants (mean [SD] age, 29.8 [5.1] years; 41 men [51.3%]) were analyzed.

facts.label: Study design and dates
facts.quote: This single-center, parallel-group RCT was conducted from November 1, 2014, to October 30, 2020.

facts.label: ClinicalTrials.gov registration
Study funding sources
facts.value: grants R01DK100426, CTSA-UL1 TR0002389, and UL1TR002389 from the National Institutes of Health
facts.quote: Funding/Support: This study was funded by grants R01DK100426, CTSA-UL1 TR0002389, and UL1TR002389 from the National Institutes of Health and by the Diabetes Research and Training Center at The University of Chicago.

facts.label: Inclusion criteria for age, BMI, and habitual sleep
facts.value: aged 21 to 40 years with a body mass index (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) between 25.0 and 29.9 and a mean habitual sleep duration of less than 6.5 hours per night
facts.quote: Adult men and women aged 21 to 40 years with a body mass index (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) between 25.0 and 29.9 and a mean habitual sleep duration of less than 6.5 hours per night were eligible.

facts.label: Required duration of stable sleep habits
facts.value: stable self-reported sleep habits for the past 6 months
facts.quote: Individuals were required to have stable self-reported sleep habits for the past 6 months.

facts.label: Screening confirmation of habitual sleep
facts.quote: Habitual sleep duration was confirmed by a 1-week screening wrist actigraphy at home.

facts.label: Exclusion criteria for sleep disorders and shift work
facts.value: obstructive sleep apnea confirmed by laboratory polysomnography (apnea-hypopnea index >5), insomnia or history of any other sleep disorder, or night shift and rotating shift work (current or in the past 2 years)
facts.quote: Those who had obstructive sleep apnea confirmed by laboratory polysomnography (apnea-hypopnea index >5), insomnia or history of any other sleep disorder, or night shift and rotating shift work (current or in the past 2 years) were excluded.

facts.label: Baseline and intervention arm durations
facts.quote: After a 2-week habitual sleep period at baseline, participants were randomized to either 2-week sleep extension (sleep extension group) or 2-week continued habitual sleep (control group) (Figure 1).

facts.label: No prescribed diet or physical activity
facts.value: without any prescribed diet or physical activity
facts.quote: Participants continued their daily routine activities at home without any prescribed diet or physical activity.

facts.label: Timing of participant blinding
facts.value: sleep extension group was blinded to randomization until after the 2-week baseline assessments, and the control group was blinded until the end of the 4-week study
facts.quote: The sleep extension group was blinded to randomization until after the 2-week baseline assessments, and the control group was blinded until the end of the 4-week study.

facts.label: Randomization blocking and stratification
facts.quote: Block randomization, stratified by sex, was performed using computer-generated random numbers.

facts.label: Wrist actigraphy device and software
facts.quote: Participants were asked to wear an accelerometer (motion)-based monitor (Actiwatch Spectrum Plus; Philips) and to press a built-in event marker button when they went to bed to sleep each night and when they got out of bed each morning.

facts.label: Sleep extension counseling and bedtime target
facts.value: extending their bedtime duration to 8.5 hours
facts.quote: At the end of the interview, participants were provided with individualized recommendations to follow at home for 2 weeks, with the aim of extending their bedtime duration to 8.5 hours.

facts.label: Mid-intervention follow-up visit
facts.value: On day 22, participants returned for a brief follow-up visit
facts.quote: On day 22, participants returned for a brief follow-up visit. Actigraphy data from the first intervention week were reviewed, and further sleep counseling was provided as needed.

facts.label: Control group investigator contact schedule
facts.quote: To minimize any imbalance in contact with the investigators between the 2 groups, we asked participants in the control group to meet with the study investigators on days 15 and 22.

facts.label: Objective assessment of energy intake
facts.value: sum of total energy expenditure and change in body energy stores
facts.quote: For each 2-week period, the energy intake was calculated from the sum of total energy expenditure and change in body energy stores using the principle of energy balance.

facts.label: Measurement of total energy expenditure
facts.quote: Total energy expenditure was measured by the doubly labeled water method.

facts.label: Assessment of change in body energy stores
facts.value: regression (slope, grams per day) of daily home weights and change in body composition (ie, fat mass and fat-free mass) using dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry
facts.quote: For each 2-week period, the change in body energy stores was computed from the regression (slope, grams per day) of daily home weights and change in body composition (ie, fat mass and fat-free mass) using dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry.

facts.label: Blinded home weight scale protocol
facts.value: Weight values were hidden from the participants
facts.quote: Participants were provided a cellular-enabled weight scale (BodyTrace; BodyTrace Inc) and instructed to take their nude weights twice every morning after awakening before eating or drinking. Weight values were hidden from the participants to minimize potential influence on behavior.

facts.label: Energy coefficients for fat and fat-free mass
facts.value: 9.5 kcal/g as the energy coefficient of fat mass and 1.0 kcal/g as the energy coefficient of fat-free mass
facts.quote: Changes in body composition were converted to changes in energy stores using 9.5 kcal/g as the energy coefficient of fat mass and 1.0 kcal/g as the energy coefficient of fat-free mass.

facts.label: Indirect calorimetry protocol for metabolic rate
facts.value: 30 minutes after fasting and for 4 hours after eating a standardized breakfast
facts.quote: Resting metabolic rate was measured by indirect calorimetry for 30 minutes after fasting and for 4 hours after eating a standardized breakfast.

facts.label: Sample size and statistical power calculation
facts.value: 80% power to detect a true difference in energy intake between groups of 207 kcal/d using a 2-sided α = .05 significance threshold
facts.quote: A total final sample size of 80 participants (40 per group) was originally planned and provided 80% power to detect a true difference in energy intake between groups of 207 kcal/d using a 2-sided α = .05 significance threshold (trial protocol in Supplement 1).

facts.label: Intention-to-treat analysis software and threshold
facts.value: intention-to-treat analysis was conducted in Stata, version 16 (StataCorp LLC) using 2-tailed tests with statistical significance set at P < .05
facts.quote: An intention-to-treat analysis was conducted in Stata, version 16 (StataCorp LLC) using 2-tailed tests with statistical significance set at P < .05.

facts.label: Secondary analyses adjusting for sex or menstrual cycle
facts.value: mixed models that adjusted for sex or menstrual cycle
facts.quote: In secondary analyses, mixed models that adjusted for sex or menstrual cycle were also fit; these covariates were chosen because of the known influence of menstrual cycle on short-term changes in weight.

facts.label: Handling of multiple comparisons and missing data
facts.value: No adjustments were made to P values or CIs for multiple comparisons
facts.quote: No adjustments were made to P values or CIs for multiple comparisons.

facts.label: Missing value imputation policy
facts.value: No imputation for missing values was performed
facts.quote: No imputation for missing values was performed.

facts.label: Number consented, screened, and initially randomized
facts.value: 210 adults who provided consent and were assessed for eligibility, 81 were randomized (41 to the control group and 40 to the sleep extension group)
facts.quote: Of the 210 adults who provided consent and were assessed for eligibility, 81 were randomized (41 to the control group and 40 to the sleep extension group) initially (Figure 1).

facts.label: Post-randomization ineligibility in control group
facts.value: One participant in the control group revealed adhering to a weight loss regimen
facts.quote: One participant in the control group revealed adhering to a weight loss regimen and thus did not meet the study inclusion criteria and was deemed ineligible after randomization.

facts.label: Overall mean (SD) age of analyzed participants
facts.quote: The 80 participants had a mean (SD) age of 29.8 (5.1) years and consisted of 41 men (51.3%) and 39 women (48.7%).

facts.label: Overall number and percentage of men
facts.quote: The 80 participants had a mean (SD) age of 29.8 (5.1) years and consisted of 41 men (51.3%) and 39 women (48.7%).

facts.label: Overall number and percentage of women
facts.quote: The 80 participants had a mean (SD) age of 29.8 (5.1) years and consisted of 41 men (51.3%) and 39 women (48.7%).

facts.label: Absence of interfering medications at baseline
facts.value: None of the participants were using any antihypertensive or lipid-lowering agents or any prescription medication that can affect sleep or metabolism
facts.quote: None of the participants were using any antihypertensive or lipid-lowering agents or any prescription medication that can affect sleep or metabolism.

Between-group difference in change in mean sleep duration
facts.quote: Participants in the sleep extension group had a significant increase from baseline in mean sleep duration by actigraphy compared with those in the control group (1.2 hours; 95% CI, 1.0-1.4 hours; P < .001).

estimate.outcome: Change from baseline in mean nightly sleep duration by actigraphy

facts.label: Between-group difference in change in sleep duration on workdays
facts.quote: The findings were similar with regard to change in sleep duration when only participants' workdays (1.3 hours; 95% CI, 1.0-1.5 hours; P < .001) or free days (1.1 hours; 95% CI, 0.7-1.5 hours; P < .001) were considered (eTable 1 in Supplement 2).

estimate.outcome: Change from baseline in sleep duration on workdays

facts.label: Between-group difference in change in sleep duration on free days
facts.quote: The findings were similar with regard to change in sleep duration when only participants' workdays (1.3 hours; 95% CI, 1.0-1.5 hours; P < .001) or free days (1.1 hours; 95% CI, 0.7-1.5 hours; P < .001) were considered (eTable 1 in Supplement 2).

estimate.outcome: Change from baseline in sleep duration on free days

facts.label: Between-group difference in change in sleep efficiency
facts.quote: No difference was found in change in sleep efficiency (percentage of time spent asleep during time in bed) between the 2 groups (–0.6 hours; 95% CI, –2.1 to 1.0 hours; P = .48), confirming the success of the intervention (eTable 2 in Supplement 2).

estimate.outcome: Change in sleep efficiency between groups

facts.label: No significant difference in sleep efficiency change
facts.quote: No difference was found in change in sleep efficiency (percentage of time spent asleep during time in bed) between the 2 groups (–0.6 hours; 95% CI, –2.1 to 1.0 hours; P = .48), confirming the success of the intervention (eTable 2 in Supplement 2).

facts.label: Correlation between change in sleep duration and change in energy intake
facts.quote: Considering all participants, the change in sleep duration was inversely correlated with the change in energy intake (r = −0.41; 95% CI, −0.59 to −0.20; P < .001) (Figure 3E).
facts.outcome: Correlation between sleep duration change and energy intake change

facts.label: Change in energy intake per 1-hour increase in sleep duration
facts.quote: Each 1-hour increase in sleep duration was associated with a decrease in energy intake of approximately 162 kcal/d (−162.3 kcal/d; 95% CI, −246.8 to −77.7 kcal/d; P < .001).
facts.outcome: Energy intake change per 1-hour sleep duration increase

facts.label: Participants with complete primary outcome data
facts.quote: No statistically significant differences in baseline characteristics were found between the 75 participants (93.8%) who had complete data on energy intake (primary outcome) vs participants with missing data on energy intake.

facts.label: Completeness of energy intake data by group
facts.quote: The proportion of participants with complete data on energy intake was not significantly different between the sleep extension and control groups (90.0% vs 97.5%; P = .36).

facts.label: Baseline differences by completeness of all outcomes
facts.value: no significant differences (except for depressive symptoms) in baseline characteristics
facts.quote: When all reported outcomes were considered, no significant differences (except for depressive symptoms) in baseline characteristics were found between participants with complete data and participants with incomplete or missing data (eTable 3 in Supplement 2).

facts.label: Completeness of all reported outcomes by group

facts.label: Subjective sleep sufficiency, energy, alertness, and mood
facts.value: significantly higher subjective scores in obtaining sufficient sleep, with more daytime energy and alertness and better mood
facts.quote: Overall, the sleep extension group compared with the control group had significantly higher subjective scores in obtaining sufficient sleep, with more daytime energy and alertness and better mood (eTable 4 in Supplement 2).
facts.outcome: Subjective sleep sufficiency, daytime energy, alertness, and mood

facts.label: US population prevalence of short sleep
facts.value: one-third of the US population reported not getting the recommended 7 to 9 hours of sleep per night
facts.quote: For example, one-third of the US population reported not getting the recommended 7 to 9 hours of sleep per night.,,,

facts.label: Dynamic prediction model for 100 kcal/d increase
facts.value: weight gain of about 4.5 kg over 3 years
facts.quote: According to dynamic prediction models, a sustained increase in energy intake of even 100 kcal/d would result in a weight gain of about 4.5 kg over 3 years.,

facts.label: Earlier lab sleep restriction studies on energy intake
facts.value: increased mean energy intake of about 250 to 350 kcal/d with minimal to no change in energy expenditure
facts.quote: Short-term experimental laboratory studies have found that sleep restriction in healthy individuals is associated with an increased mean energy intake of about 250 to 350 kcal/d with minimal to no change in energy expenditure.,,,

facts.label: Hall dynamic prediction model for 270 kcal/d reduction
facts.value: approximately 12-kg weight loss over 3 years if the effects were sustained over a long term
facts.quote: According to the Hall dynamic prediction model, a decrease in energy intake of approximately 270 kcal/d, which we observed after short-term sleep extension, would predict an approximately 12-kg weight loss over 3 years if the effects were sustained over a long term.,

facts.label: Meta-analysis of lab sleep restriction RCTs
facts.value: increases of mean energy intake by approximately 253 kcal/d
facts.quote: A recent meta-analysis of randomized controlled laboratory studies found that short-term sleep restriction over 1 to 14 days of duration in healthy individuals was associated with increases of mean energy intake by approximately 253 kcal/d, as assessed during a single meal.

facts.label: Meta-analysis of prospective cohorts on sleep and obesity
facts.value: risk of obesity increased by 9% for each 1-hour decrease in sleep duration
facts.quote: Another meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies found that the risk of obesity increased by 9% for each 1-hour decrease in sleep duration.

facts.label: Prior whole-room calorimeter studies on total energy expenditure
facts.value: increase in total energy expenditure of approximately 92 to 111 kcal/d
facts.quote: Although some laboratory sleep-restriction studies reported an increase in total energy expenditure of approximately 92 to 111 kcal/d, using a whole-room calorimeter,, other studies observed no change.,

facts.label: Prior observations on 7 to 8 hours sleep and weight loss success
facts.value: sleeping 7 to 8 hours per night is associated with greater success in weight loss interventions
facts.quote: A few observations suggest that sleeping 7 to 8 hours per night is associated with greater success in weight loss interventions.,,,

facts.label: Limited generalizability due to selective eligibility
facts.value: enrolled adults with overweight and used selective eligibility criteria, which may limit generalizability to more diverse populations
facts.quote: We enrolled adults with overweight and used selective eligibility criteria, which may limit generalizability to more diverse populations.

facts.label: Control group increases may have contributed to treatment effects
facts.value: increase in energy intake and weight from baseline that we observed in the control group may have contributed to the significant treatment effects
facts.quote: The increase in energy intake and weight from baseline that we observed in the control group may have contributed to the significant treatment effects.

facts.label: Unknown long-term sustainability of sleep habits
facts.value: did not provide information on how long healthy sleep habits could be maintained over longer periods
facts.quote: The study did not provide information on how long healthy sleep habits could be maintained over longer periods.

facts.label: Factors influencing sleep behavior not systematically assessed
facts.value: did not systematically assess the factors that may have influenced sleep behavior
facts.quote: We did not systematically assess the factors that may have influenced sleep behavior, but limiting the use of electronic devices appeared to be a key intervention among the participants (eTable 4 in Supplement 2).

facts.quote: We did not assess the underlying biological mechanisms of food frequency and the circadian timing of food intake.

facts.label: Need for longer-duration studies in diverse populations
facts.value: Future similarly rigorous intervention studies of longer duration and using objective assessments of energy balance under real-life conditions are warranted
facts.quote: Future similarly rigorous intervention studies of longer duration and using objective assessments of energy balance under real-life conditions are warranted to elucidate the underlying mechanisms and to investigate whether sleep extension could be an effective, scalable strategy for reversing obesity in diverse populations.

facts.label: Sleep hygiene counseling delivery
facts.value: individualized sleep hygiene counseling through a structured interview
facts.quote: Those who were randomized to the sleep extension group received individualized sleep hygiene counseling through a structured interview (E.T.) (eMethods in Supplement 2).

facts.label: Control group instructions
facts.value: did not receive any specific sleep recommendations and were instructed to continue their daily routine and habitual sleep behaviors
facts.quote: Actigraphy data of these participants were downloaded, but the participants did not receive any specific sleep recommendations and were instructed to continue their daily routine and habitual sleep behaviors until the end of the study.

facts.label: Sleep monitoring duration
facts.quote: Sleep-wake patterns were continuously monitored at home by wrist actigraphy throughout the 4-week study.

facts.label: Baseline habitual sleep instruction
facts.quote: During the 2-week baseline, all participants were instructed to continue their habitual sleep patterns at home.

facts.label: Prior real-life bedtime extension study
facts.quote: Another study used bedtime extension in habitual short sleepers in real-life conditions but obtained variable benefits on sleep, likely because of a lack of an individualized approach or appropriate blinding.

facts.label: Further understanding of population energy intake factors
facts.quote: Factors that underlie the observed persistent increase in energy intake and mean weight gain at the population level need to be better understood.
